name: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn
aliases: subcutaneous fat necrosis of the neonate

clinicalPearls: Presents in the first weeks of life as firm, indurated, red to violaceous nodules and plaques over the back, buttocks, shoulders, thighs and cheeks
It typically follows a difficult delivery, perinatal hypoxia, hypothermia, therapeutic cooling or other perinatal stress in an otherwise term or post-term infant
Lesions are usually painless or mildly tender and the baby is generally well at presentation
The most important complication is hypercalcaemia, which may appear weeks after the skin lesions and can be dangerous
Biopsy shows a lobular panniculitis with needle-shaped clefts within adipocytes and a granulomatous infiltrate with multinucleate giant cells
Affected infants need monitoring of serum calcium for several weeks to months even as the skin improves
Skin lesions resolve spontaneously, so treatment is largely supportive with active management of any hypercalcaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn is an injury to neonatal fat that follows perinatal stresses such as hypoxia, hypothermia and trauma, often in the setting of therapeutic hypothermia. Neonatal fat is rich in saturated fatty acids with a higher solidification point, making it prone to crystallisation and necrosis when subjected to cold or ischaemia. The damaged adipocytes provoke a granulomatous inflammatory response with characteristic needle-shaped crystal clefts. Granulomatous tissue can produce excess 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, driving intestinal calcium absorption and the delayed hypercalcaemia that is the key systemic risk.
additionalInvestigations: Serial serum calcium measurement over subsequent weeks to months
Serum phosphate, and vitamin D metabolites if hypercalcaemia occurs
Renal function and, if calcium is high, renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis
Skin biopsy for the characteristic crystalline lobular panniculitis when uncertain
Full blood count and platelet count (thrombocytopenia may occur)
Glucose and triglycerides in extensive disease
redFlags: Hypercalcaemia with poor feeding, vomiting, irritability, lethargy or seizures
Nephrocalcinosis or renal impairment from sustained hypercalcaemia
Extensive or ulcerating lesions with possible secondary infection
reference.prognosis: The skin lesions almost always resolve spontaneously over weeks to months, sometimes with transient atrophy; the outlook is good provided hypercalcaemia is detected and managed, as untreated hypercalcaemia can cause significant morbidity.
pitfalls: Discharging without arranging prolonged calcium monitoring, so delayed hypercalcaemia is missed
Mistaking the firm plaques for cellulitis and giving unnecessary antibiotics
Confusing it with the more diffuse and ominous sclerema neonatorum
Assuming resolution of the skin signals that the risk of hypercalcaemia has passed
management: Manage the skin lesions conservatively, as the nodules resolve spontaneously and need only supportive skin care
Monitor serum calcium serially over weeks to months, because dangerous hypercalcaemia is characteristically delayed after the skin lesions appear
Treat significant hypercalcaemia with intravenous fluid rehydration and a loop diuretic to enhance calcium excretion
Use corticosteroids to reduce granulomatous 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production, with calcitonin or a bisphosphonate for refractory cases
Restrict calcium and vitamin D intake and withhold vitamin D supplementation during the at-risk period
Check renal function and arrange renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis, and monitor the platelet count for thrombocytopenia
Involve neonatology and paediatric endocrinology to manage hypercalcaemia and its complications
